```{r a6-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

An analysis result records grade membership, disclosed and withheld pairs,
expected loss and the numerical evidence for optimality. These components
have distinct interpretations and should remain associated when results are
exported. We describe the console summaries and result tables, followed by
formats for retaining an analysis or producing a readable report.

The examples use the six fictional sites in
[Analysis with one or several criteria](a1-getting-started.html). Their normal score distributions
are specified, with larger scores receiving higher priority. The first
analysis uses one criterion and the second adds a criterion for the same
sites. The prepared results below require neither optimization nor model
fitting during rendering.

```{r a6-load}
library(postrank)
sites <- pr_tutorial
```

```{r a6-prepared, include=FALSE}
source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package = "postrank",
  mustWork = TRUE), local = TRUE)
one <- load_or_compute("tutorial_one")
two <- load_or_compute("tutorial_two")
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

The objects `one` and `two` are prepared analyses corresponding to the calls
in the introductory analysis. The same inspection and export functions apply to other
analyses returned by `postrank()`.

## Console output and interpretation {#read-the-result-before-taking-a-column}

```{r a6-print}
print(one)
```

The initial display gives the numbers of entities and grades, disclosed
and withheld pair counts, and computation status. Grade 1 has highest
priority; a shared grade withholds a comparison without declaring score
equality. Since the reported loss depends on the weights, withholding cost
and permitted grades, these settings are part of the interpretation of any
exported risk.

```{r a6-summary}
summary(one)
```

The summary adds settings, criterion-specific results, bounds and recorded
warnings. Monte Carlo fragility is unsupported here because the input
specifies an analytic normal law rather than target draws. An unsupported
diagnostic differs from one that was available but not requested. Neither
state implies a zero value, and the summary does not calculate missing
results.

The first prepared solve includes a small floating-point correction to its
lower bound. The summary retains the warning despite a zero reported gap
after correction. Further source records and identifiers are available by
requesting detailed output:

```{r a6-details}
detailed <- summary(one, details = TRUE)
```

Printing `detailed` displays the additional records identifying the input
and computation. Numerical extraction uses the accessors below rather than
parsing the console representation.

## Grade and report-card tables {#take-a-stable-grade-table}

```{r a6-basic-table}
grade_table <- as.data.frame(one)
grade_table
```

The default table has two columns: character `entity_id` and integer
`grade`. Rows follow the original input order. A fit, its enclosing
analysis, and a score-cut baseline use this same basic form. Optional
report cards do not change the default columns.

```{r a6-table-checks}
identical(grade_table$entity_id, sites$one$entity_ids)
identical(grade_table, as.data.frame(one$fit))
```

The `entity_id` column provides the key for joining results to other tables.
Row numbers and potentially changing display names do not serve this role.
A separately sorted copy may be used for presentation while the original
table retains its correspondence with input order.

The report-card table is requested explicitly:

```{r a6-card-table}
card <- as.data.frame(one, what = "report_card")
knitr::kable(card[c("entity_id", "grade", "mean_score_A",
  "lower_score_A", "upper_score_A")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Entity", "Grade", "Mean", "Interval lower", "Interval upper"))
```

The table contains prepared score means and
`r fmt(100 * one$report_card$level, 0)`% equal-tail marginal intervals under
the specified normal law. These describe score uncertainty rather than
uncertainty in grade labels. Expected ranks and disclosed and withheld
comparison counts are also included. Selection by column name avoids
dependence on column positions.

Report-card rows are ordered by grade and their recorded secondary order.
That can differ from input order, as the two-criterion example shows:

```{r a6-order}
list(
  input_order = as.data.frame(two)$entity_id,
  report_card_order = as.data.frame(two, what = "report_card")$entity_id
)
```

If a report card was not prepared, `what = "report_card"` reports the reason
for its absence, while the ordinary grade table may remain available.
Pairwise probabilities can suffice for grading without identifying marginal
intervals. Supplied intervals retain their original level, such as the 95%
intervals in the [Alabama case](a4-alabama-opportunity.html). Table conversion
neither creates missing summaries nor changes an interval's level.

For code written before version 1.0, the explicit `what = "report_card"`
replaces the former behavior in which an analysis could return its full
card by default. The default table therefore retains the two-column
structure described above.

## Grades, pair relations and loss {#extract-grades-pair-relations-and-loss}

```{r a6-accessors}
grades <- get_grades(one)
grades
relations <- get_relations(one)
relations[c("A", "B", "C"), c("A", "B", "C")]
```

The grade vector is named by entity ID. In the relation matrix, `[i, j]` is
1 if row entity `i` is disclosed above column entity `j`, −1 for the reverse
direction and 0 for withholding. The diagonal is zero. Thus A versus B is
withheld and A is disclosed above C. Matrix entries represent reporting
decisions rather than posterior probabilities.

```{r a6-profile}
profile <- get_profile(one)
knitr::kable(profile[c("criterion", "weight", "E", "E_over_M",
  "E_over_N", "risk")], digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)
risk <- get_risk(one)
risk
```

`E` is the posterior expected number of wrong-direction comparisons among
the disclosed pairs. `E_over_N` divides by the number of disclosed pairs;
`E_over_M` divides by all possible pairs. The criterion's `risk` also
includes the cost of withholding. For this one-criterion example, the
criterion loss and the overall loss are the same:

```{r a6-loss}
N <- sum(relations[upper.tri(relations)] != 0L)
M <- choose(length(grades), 2)
loss_from_parts <- (profile$E + one$settings$tau * (M - N)) / M
c(from_parts = loss_from_parts, stored = risk$risk)
```

For several criteria, `get_profile(two)` returns one row per criterion;
equal weights can yield different error rates. `get_risk()` returns a list
containing `risk`, `lower_bound`, `gap` and `status`. The risk is the primary
objective of the specified problem: a weighted average of criterion losses
in these examples, or a worst-criterion objective in minimax analyses.
Comparison of reported losses therefore requires their objective definitions.

For the same one-criterion input, the following calculation evaluates the
fixed action withholding every pair, without a new optimization:

```{r a6-all-withheld}
withheld <- postrank_evaluate(
  setNames(rep(1L, length(grades)), names(grades)), sites$one,
  weights = c(score_A = 1), tau = one$settings$tau
)
withheld[c("N", "E_over_N", "primary_risk")]
```

Since no comparisons are disclosed, `E_over_N` is `NA` and the loss equals
the withholding cost. This is a valid grading with an undefined error
proportion, distinct from a computation that returned no valid grade vector.

## Computation status and numerical results {#keep-computation-status-with-the-numbers}

The prepared examples have `optimal` status. In other analyses, computation
may terminate before establishing optimality. Whether validated grades exist
must also be considered when interpreting status. The table describes
possible states; it does not report additional solver executions.

| Recorded state | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `optimal`, with validated grades | Optimal within the recorded solver tolerances. The bound, gap and any numerical warnings provide the accompanying numerical evidence. |
| `feasible_not_certified`, with validated grades | A usable grading was found, but the available bound or gap does not establish the requested optimality. |
| `time_limit`, with validated grades | The time limit was reached; the stored grading can be read and evaluated, with its remaining gap or missing bound disclosed. |
| `time_limit`, without validated grades | There is no grading to interpret. The termination status and any usable lower bound can still be reported. |
| `infeasible` | The solver reports that the requested constraints cannot be satisfied. This is not a one-grade, all-withheld result. |

Results with `numerical_error`, `unknown` or an unexpected `unbounded`
status require examination of recorded warnings and validation details
before an action is used. Normalized status records the package's
interpretation separately from the backend message. A gap quantifies
optimization uncertainty conditional on the supplied probabilities, rather
than posterior uncertainty about a population quantity.

In the absence of validated grades, `get_grades()` and `get_relations()`
return `NULL`. The basic table and criterion profile have zero rows with
their usual columns. `get_risk()` retains status and any usable lower bound,
whereas action risk and gap are `NA`. An empty result thus requires
interpretation of the recorded status; assigning all entities to grade 1
would introduce an action that the computation did not return.

## Tabular export and object storage {#save-a-table-and-preserve-an-analysis}

CSV stores tabular output, whereas RDS retains the complete R object,
including settings, summaries and computation records. The examples use a
new temporary directory to avoid overwriting existing files:

```{r a6-export-folder}
export_dir <- tempfile("postrank-exports-")
dir.create(export_dir)
csv_file <- file.path(export_dir, "grades.csv")
rds_file <- file.path(export_dir, "analysis.rds")
```

```{r a6-csv}
write.csv(grade_table, csv_file, row.names = FALSE)
csv_again <- read.csv(csv_file,
  colClasses = c(entity_id = "character", grade = "integer"))
identical(csv_again, grade_table)
```

A character ID column preserves leading zeros in identifiers such as
`"01001"`, and `row.names = FALSE` omits an additional row-index column.
Interval definitions, settings and solver status must be exported
separately when CSV is used for a report table.

```{r a6-rds}
saveRDS(one, rds_file)
restored <- readRDS(rds_file)
identical(get_grades(restored), grades)
identical(get_risk(restored), risk)
identical(as.data.frame(restored, what = "report_card"), card)
```

Reading the RDS restores the prepared object without rerunning the
optimizer. Reproducibility additionally requires the package version and
source input. RDS is an R object format whose compatibility with every
future software version cannot be assumed.

## Standalone HTML reports {#write-a-standalone-html-report}

Supplying a fit together with its matching analysis includes the prepared
posterior report card alongside grades, loss, status and available
diagnostics:

```{r a6-html-report}
html_file <- file.path(export_dir, "grades-report.html")
report <- postrank_report(one$fit, analysis = one,
  output_file = html_file, lang = "en")
report
basename(report$output_file)
```

The English HTML report embeds its figures for offline reading and uses
stored results throughout. Missing intervals or diagnostics retain their
recorded reasons for unavailability. An existing destination is refused,
so each saved version requires a new filename. Setting `figures = FALSE`
produces text and tables without embedded figures.

The temporary directory persists for the current R session. Longer-term
storage requires a new destination within the project. RDS retains the
analysis for subsequent R use, HTML provides a readable report and CSV
provides selected tables for other software.

Figure dimensions, labels and entity selection are described in
[Figures and sensitivity analysis](a7-figures-sensitivity.html). Input
assumptions are discussed in
[Analysis of supplied posterior results](a5-your-posterior-results.html).

[Computing grades and choosing settings](m5-computing-grades.html) develops the meaning of solver bounds and admissible reports. [Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics](m6-uncertainty-diagnostics.html) covers the distinct numerical uncertainty in the posterior inputs.
